fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Moses says the LORD brought them out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, “…to be the people of His inheritance, as you are today.” The furnace is where they had been. The inheritance is who they belong to now. The LORD didn't only get them out. He took them as His own.

Right, friend. Moses says that if they act corruptly and make an idol, “You will not live long upon it, but will be utterly destroyed.” He even calls heaven and earth as witnesses before he says it. That's a heavy warning, and he states it plainly so nobody can miss it.

Distant isn't the word Moses uses here. He says the LORD is “…a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers…” Merciful is what fills the blank. Earlier Moses asked what nation has a god as near as the LORD is to Israel whenever they call on Him.

Yes, friend. Moses says, “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him.” That's the reason, plain and simple. The trials, signs, wonders and war were all shown for that. Nothing added.

Freedom isn't the reason Moses gives here. He says the statutes and ordinances are so Israel may live and take possession of the land the LORD is giving them. The LORD is the one giving the land. Moses keeps the reason simple, and so should we.

Moses does mention himself in that verse, but only as the one teaching the statutes and ordinances. The reason he gives is “…so that you may live and may enter and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you.” Keeping him as leader isn't in it. Later he says outright that he will not be crossing the Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:22). So the reason points to the people living in the land.

Right, friend. Moses says, “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you…” Nothing gets added and nothing gets cut. The commands stay just as the LORD gave them. Moses says the point is that they may keep the commandments of the LORD their God.

That's what Moses says. “But you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day, every one of you.” Every single one, with nobody missing. Just before that, he says the LORD destroyed all who followed Baal of Peor, a false god. Those who followed him were destroyed, and those who held fast are alive.
Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Moses says those who held fast to the LORD “…are alive to this day, every one of you.” The word he lands on is alive. And he says it right to the people listening.

Fierce and fearless sounds like a movie trailer, friend. But Moses says the peoples will hear of all these statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” Nobody in that line is talking about swords. They hear the statutes and say wise. They never say scary.

Hidden is a fair guess, but it isn't what Moses says. The word is near: a god “…as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him?” Moses is marveling at how close the LORD is when Israel calls. That's the point of the question.

Moses does call the statutes righteous in the very next verse. But strict isn't the word in this blank. This blank is about how close the LORD is. Moses asks what nation has a god “…as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him?”

Yes, friend. Moses says the LORD declared “…His covenant, which He commanded you to follow—the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone.” The LORD wrote them on stone Himself. That's about as clear as it gets.

Tribes isn't the word in this verse. Moses says the LORD declared His covenant, “…the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone.” What went on the tablets was the Ten Commandments. That's the word that fills the blank.

A treaty with the nations? Friend, that's a whole other sermon. The warning here is about an idol: “…do not act corruptly and make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape…” The reason comes right before it. At Horeb they saw no form, only a voice, so Moses tells them to be careful.

That's right. Moses says he must die in this land, but then adds, “But you shall cross over and take possession of that good land.” He's not crossing, but the people are. I think that was a heavy thing for him to say out loud, and he says it plainly.

Moses steps right out of the spotlight here. He says, “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him.” The point of what they saw was to know who God is. Moses isn't the answer to that.

Yes, friend. Moses says, “Keep His statutes and commandments, which I am giving you today, so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time.” That's the sermon brought home. Moses names their children right in the verse, so this reaches past that one generation.
